facts.fact: Freshly hatched Artemia nauplii, rinsed free of salt, are a live food for newly hatched fish fry.
Dry Artemia cysts stay metabolically inactive while dry. Once soaked in salt water they hydrate and the embryo resumes development.
Instar I nauplii are about 400-500 µm long and do not feed. They live on their yolk reserves.
Nauplii molt to instar II after about 8 h and then start feeding on particles of about 1-50 µm.
The cyst's outer membrane usually bursts after about 20 h ('breaking'). An 'umbrella' stage follows, then the free-swimming nauplius is released.
When aeration stops, the nauplii gather as a reddish layer just above the bottom. Unhatched eggs sink and empty shells rise within 5-8 minutes.
After 12-15 h embryos start to emerge and hang under the shell. By 24 h nauplii swim freely.
Nauplii are attracted to light and swim toward it.
Use a transparent jar or pot of 1-4 litres with a diameter of no more than 13-16 cm.
A conical-bottom container aerated from the bottom works best. Cylindrical or square containers develop dead spots.
An upside-down 2-litre plastic bottle can serve as a home hatching cone.
Salt water: about 30 g NaCl per litre (28-30 ppt), roughly 1 tablespoon of kitchen salt per litre of tap water.
Aquarium Co-op recipe: about 2 litres of water, 2 tablespoons of aquarium salt (or marine salt for soft water) and up to 1 tablespoon of eggs.
Aquarium Co-op adds 1-2 drops of dechlorinator if the tap water contains chloramine.
Without seawater, dissolve 30 g of non-iodized coarse salt in 1 litre of water. Dechlorinate tap water first by aerating it.
Low-salt alternative (Wilkerson): 2 teaspoons of cheap coarse salt in 2 litres of dechlorinated tap water, aerated about 1 hour before adding eggs.
Optimal hatching salinity is generally 5-35 g/l. Lower salinity speeds hatching.
Cyst density: 1-3 teaspoons of cysts per litre.
Cyst density: up to 5 g/l for volumes under 20 l, and at most 2 g/l for larger volumes.
Use about 1 g of eggs per litre. For a 2-litre bottle, roughly 1/4 teaspoon of eggs is enough.
Temperature: keep the water at 25-28°C. Below 25°C cysts hatch more slowly.
Incubation temperature: 22-30°C.
Keep the hatchery at 74-82°F (23-28°C) using room heat, a small incandescent or halogen lamp, or a small heater, and wait longer if it is cool.
Keep pH above 8, ideally 8-8.5. Add sodium bicarbonate if needed: up to 2 g/l on the FAO worksheet, or up to 1 g/l in another section of the same manual.
Light: about 2000 lux at the water surface, especially in the first hours after the cysts are fully hydrated.
A lamp placed about 20 cm above the water surface can supply the light.
Aerate continuously and strongly enough to keep the eggs from settling.
Keep dissolved oxygen above 2 mg/l, preferably 5 mg/l.
Put a rigid plastic tube at the lowest point of the container instead of an airstone. Ease the airflow once eggs swell so bubbles don't carry them out.
In the standard test (33 g/l, 25°C) the first nauplii appear after 12-16 h. 90% should have hatched within 24 h.
Hatching is complete after 20-24 hours, depending on temperature.
Harvest: stop aeration, remove the airstone and carefully siphon the nauplii layer near the bottom without taking eggs or shells.
Harvest: turn off the pump and shine a light near the bottom outlet to draw the shrimp there, then open the valve.
Skim floating shells off with a fine net, then siphon the nauplii with a tube about 3 mm in diameter.
Filter siphoned nauplii through a 100-150 µm plankton net and rinse out the salt before feeding fry.
Aquarium Co-op notes you can feed the nauplii with their salt water if the tank has live plants that need minerals or hard-water fish.
Start a new batch around day 2, since one batch is used up in 2-3 days of feeding.
Decapsulation: first hydrate cysts for about 1 h in water under 100 g/l, with aeration, at 25°C.
Decapsulation dose: 0.5 g active hypochlorite per g of cysts, plus 0.15 g NaOH per g of cysts with liquid bleach to keep pH above 10. Final volume is 14 ml per g of cysts.
Keep decapsulation at 15-20°C and never above 40°C, because the reaction gives off heat. Add ice if needed. It takes about 3-15 min, until the shell dissolves.
Liquid bleach turns cysts orange during decapsulation, while bleaching powder turns them grey.
After decapsulation, rinse until no chlorine smell remains. Neutralize with a dip of under 1 min in 0.1% sodium thiosulfate (or 0.1 N HCl).
Disinfection without decapsulation: about 200 ppm hypochlorite for 30 min. This does not kill all germs in the shell.
Decapsulated cysts keep their hatchability for a few days at 0-4°C.
Store dry cysts cool, ideally under vacuum or nitrogen, because oxygen damages them.
Avoid repeated wetting and drying of cysts. Protect cysts from direct sunlight, since UV lowers hatchability.
Frozen cysts should sit at least one week at room temperature before use.
Unhatched eggs stored cold can be used for 6 months to 1 year.
Harvest when about 90% have hatched to get nauplii with the most energy. Late harvest gives a mix of instar I, II and III.
Shells or unhatched eggs eaten by small fish can block the gut and kill them. Decapsulation removes this risk.
Insufficient aeration or dead spots in square or cylindrical containers lowers hatching.
Temperatures above 33°C stop cyst metabolism irreversibly.
Putting too many cysts per litre lowers the hatch rate.
Hatching in shade or with too little light lowers the hatch rate.
Too much aeration causes foaming.
Leaving cysts too long in hypochlorite or letting decapsulation exceed 40°C kills the embryos. Leftover chlorine is also harmful.
Using an airstone instead of a rigid tube, or aerating hard after eggs swell, blows eggs out of the bottle.
Feeding nauplii too late: for very small fry use nauplii under about 30 h old. After about 24 h the yolk is used up.
Forum members cite too much or too little salt, harvesting too late and using old eggs as causes of poor results.
Use non-iodized coarse salt (muối hột), not iodized table salt.
Power cuts can endanger incubation, because aeration must run continuously.
Vietnamese guides recommend muối hột (non-iodized coarse/sea salt) for keepers without natural seawater, especially in the South.
A Vietnamese guide says O.S.I. eggs imported from the US (Century, Phoenix, Crystal, Petrel brands) hatch in about 12 h, with up to 95% hatching ('bung dù').
Harvest at about 8 h (about 500 µm, orange-red) for 3-day-old betta fry. Older nauplii suit larger fry and small fish such as guppies, neon tetras and angelfish.
A 1.5 L plastic soft-drink bottle (chai Pepsi) can be used as a home hatching bottle.
Vietnamese hobbyists often split bulk egg packs between several people because small packs are rarely sold. A fine harvest net can be sewn from white cloth.
Vĩnh Châu (Sóc Trăng) and Bạc Liêu are Vietnam's main Artemia cyst producing areas. A Cần Thơ University study hatched Vĩnh Châu cysts at 30‰, 3 g/L, with continuous aeration and neon lights.
Vietnam's tropical heat needs watching: Artemia survival dropped sharply at 34°C in a Cần Thơ University study.
Some hobbyists doubt that shells cause gut blockage in fry. One forum user puts the risk at roughly 1 in 1,000 fry, but UF/IFAS treats it as a real risk.
Hatch rate and speed vary between batches because of how cysts were harvested, processed and stored. Test each new batch before relying on it.
